description: Language Starter phrases. One entry per phrase and language. n = fixed phrase number (never changes, new phrases get 46, 47...). text or forms {m, f} (speaker gender). translit = Latin spelling for non-Latin scripts. {X} = placeholder for a name or place. checked = reviewed by a native speaker. EN entries carry meaning (note for translators) and gender: true where the speaker's gender can change the words.

phrases.note: Elative -st, attached without a hyphen in normal writing (Soomest, Itaaliast); country names ending in -maa take -lt instead (Saksamaalt, Inglismaalt), and foreign names may add a vowel (Berliinist).
The ending follows vowel harmony (-sta/-stä) and is attached without a hyphen; the stem can change (Englanti: Englannista, Suomi: Suomesta) and a few names take -lta/-ltä (Venäjältä).
Finnish has no separate word for please: when asking for something you add kiitos (Kahvi, kiitos), so it is the same word as thank you.
Natural answer to sorry; as an answer to thanks Finns usually say Ei kestä.
Before a vowel 'de' becomes 'd'' (d'Italie); many countries take an article: du Portugal, des Pays-Bas. Cities and feminine countries use plain 'de' (de Paris, de France).
Informal. To a waiter or a stranger French speakers say 's'il vous plaît'.
Chosen because it is gender-neutral. 'I'm sorry' as 'Désolé' / 'Désolée' would need speaker forms.
France usage. In Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec the midday meal is 'le dîner'.

'glücklich' is fairly strong (deep happiness); for 'glad right now' natives also say 'Ich bin froh' or 'Ich freue mich'.

The suffix follows vowel harmony: -ból (Németországból), -ből (Berlinből). Hungarian towns and cities usually take -ról/-ről (Budapestről, Szegedről). In normal writing it is attached without a hyphen.
Szia is used for both hello and goodbye; Viszlát is an alternative for goodbye.
Kérlek is the informal please when asking someone; when ordering, Hungarians say kérek (Egy kávét kérek).
Fine with names; a common noun needs the article a/az (Hol van a pályaudvar?).
Most place names follow "as" unchanged (as Éirinn, as Corcaigh), but many country names take the article and then eclipsis: as an nGearmáin, as an bhFrainc, as an Spáinn (no eclipsis on s).
Irish has no single word for yes; answers normally repeat the verb (Tá / Is ea / Ba ea). "Sea" is the usual all-purpose short yes.
Irish has no single word for no; answers normally repeat the verb negatively (Níl / Ní hea / Níor). "Ní hea" is the usual all-purpose short no.

phrases.note: Unsure which call is most natural when shouted; "Fóir orm!" or "Cabhraigh liom!" (help me) are also used.
Fine for cities (Vengo da Roma). Countries take the article: dalla Francia, dal Portogallo, dall'Italia, dagli Stati Uniti.
"no" takes the genitive: the place name changes its ending (Latvija -> no Latvijas, Rīga -> no Rīgas); indeclinable foreign names stay unchanged.
"iš" takes the genitive: the place name changes its ending (Lietuva -> iš Lietuvos, Vilnius -> iš Vilniaus).
Past-tense verb (I got lost), gender-neutral and the most natural wording; the participle form would be Aš pasiklydęs / pasiklydusi.
Young Maltese mostly greet with the English loan "Hello" (Maltese spelling Ħello) or "Ċaw"; "Bonġu" is also used as hello until about midday.
Not fully sure this is the most common wording; the short "Pjaċir" is also very common.
With country names that take the article, minn + il- contracts: mill-Ġermanja, mill-Italja (but minn Malta, minn Franza).
Many young people would just say the loanword "Brejk!".
Literally "the meal is ready"; "L-ikel lest" (the food is ready) is also common. Unsure which a group leader would shout more.
Spelling of the loanword varies (tojlit / toilet); "il-kamra tal-banju" (bathroom) is also used.
Verb agrees with the thing liked: jogħġobni for a masculine thing, togħġobni for a feminine one.
"hu" agrees with a masculine place (Fejn hu l-istazzjon?); use "hi" for a feminine one (Fejn hi l-knisja?).
Polish has no separate informal morning greeting; Dzień dobry is used all day and sounds polite. Peers usually just say Cześć.

Many places take the article and contract: Sou da Alemanha, do Brasil, dos Estados Unidos, do Porto. Plain 'de' for Portugal, Lisboa, Espanha.

Spain usage: 'la comida' is the midday meal. In Latin America it is 'el almuerzo' (in Spain 'almuerzo' is a mid-morning snack).
'Snälla' is used when asking someone to do something. When ordering or asking for a thing, Swedes add 'tack' instead (En kaffe, tack).

phrases.note: In Norway 112 reaches the police; ambulance is 113 and fire 110 (112 still works from any phone).
Icelanders say 'Góðan daginn' (good day) in the morning too; 'Góðan morgun' exists but is much less common.
'frá' takes the dative, so the place name changes: frá Þýskalandi (Þýskaland), frá Póllandi (Pólland).
Sounds formal; in everyday speech Icelanders usually just add 'takk' after a request instead of a word for 'please'.
'Pása' is the everyday spoken word; 'Hlé' is the more formal standard word.
Gender-neutral plural, common today; the traditional form is 'Allir saman!' (masculine generic).
Proper names take the suffix after an apostrophe; it follows vowel harmony and the last sound: 'danım (Almanya'danım), 'denim (Türkiye'denim), 'tanım/'tenim after voiceless consonants (Paris'tenim).

The ablative ending depends on the place name: most names take -იდან (ბერლინიდან, გერმანიიდან, საფრანგეთიდან), names ending in -ო/-ე/-უ take -დან (ტოკიოდან). In normal writing it is attached without a hyphen.
Among friends კარგად (kargad, lit. be well) is also a very common bye.
When ordering or asking for something, თუ შეიძლება (tu sheidzleba, lit. if possible) is also very common.
Fits as an answer to sorry; as an answer to thanks Georgians usually say არაფრის (arapris).
Lit. I didn't catch it: the usual reply when you did not understand what was just said; the present-tense alternative is არ მესმის (ar mesmis).

Ablative -ից; after names ending in a vowel (-ա, -ո) it becomes -յից (Գերմանիայից, Իտալիայից). With Armenian-script names it is attached without a hyphen (Բեռլինից); the hyphen is used after Latin-script names.
Also very common: Կենացդ (to you, one person) or Առողջություն (to health).
Fine with names; a common noun takes the article -ը/-ն (Որտե՞ղ է կայարանը).
The ending follows vowel harmony: -danam after back vowels (Almaniyadanam), -dənəm after front vowels (Berlindənəm). In normal writing it is attached without a hyphen.

"o" causes soft mutation of Welsh place names (Caerdydd -> o Gaerdydd, Llundain -> o Lundain); foreign names usually stay unchanged (o Ffrainc, o Berlin).
Informal ti-form as the spec requires; the fixed formula "Os gwelwch yn dda" is far more common in everyday use, and young people often just say "plîs".

Welsh has no single word for yes; answers repeat the verb (Ydw, Oes, Do...). "Ie" is the general short yes.
Welsh has no single word for no; answers repeat the verb negatively (Nac ydw, Nac oes, Naddo...). "Na" is the general short no.

phrases.note: n-rule (Eifeler Regel): the final n stays before a vowel or h, d, t, z, n (Ech heeschen Anna, Ech heeschen Tom) and is dropped before other consonants (Ech heesche Marie).
Countries with an article take it after "aus": aus der Schwäiz, aus den USA, aus der Tierkei; most others are bare (aus Lëtzebuerg, aus Frankräich).
Usual word after bumping into someone; for a real apology "Et deet mer leed" (I'm sorry).
Standalone form keeps the n by the n-rule; "Nee" is also widely written and said. Not fully sure which the current dictionary (LOD) treats as primary.
Plural address to the group; "Komm, mir fänken un!" is an equally common alternative.
